cells.tense: The pull arrives, and what it holds is being read while it is still arriving.
cells.act: count it out and read what the numbers show
cells.ask: Choose one person. Each time the pull shows up around them, make a mark on paper — a mark, not a note. Read the marks once there are enough of them to hold together.
cells.core:
What you gather, you gather without inflating. Somebody comes into the room and before either of you speaks you already hold several versions of what they might be feeling — not as a strain, as information. You are sitting in the middle of that material all day and handling it well. Nothing is running ahead of you here.

Here is the part that pays. Choose one person and make a mark each time the pull shows up around them. Marks only, no words — that is the whole practice. Read the marks once there are enough to hold together. Not for a verdict, just to hear what they show. Your counting gets trusted as evidence, and it holds. The tally has its own thing to tell you about who that person is.
cells.sheetLine: What you gather before anyone speaks, you gather clean.
cells.verb: gathering everything another person might feel into one pull
cells.place: a small steady practice, in the room where the body keeps its own counsel

cells.tense: Soon, the practice will be braced against a future the person cannot write in yet.
cells.act: set the finished thing down in a form that keeps
cells.ask: One bond you keep polished toward its better version — leave it this week at the size it already is. No next step, no promise added.
cells.core:
There is nothing wrong with wanting the possibilities. The trouble shows up as technique. You are drawing that practice toward a brightened version of whoever is across the table — the talk rehearsed forward, the other person kept in the best light they could take on. The plain face at the plain hour rarely gets through.

A practice is smallest at its most settled. Pick one bond that is already good, and this week hold it at the size it is. Do not improve it and do not end it; let it stay this. A practice that can sit still is stronger than one that keeps rehearsing. The two of you get to know what the room looks like when nothing is climbing. What is here outlasts what is only on its way, and holding it still will show you that.

cells.tense: The practice stood at a door it has not used and still has its hand on the latch.
cells.act: put the problem down and take a walk with nothing to solve
cells.ask: Nothing is waiting on you where you stand. Step outside for a stretch with no one to figure out and nothing to settle. Come back empty-handed.
cells.core:
Your practice is steady and shows up every week. Something in it has stopped expecting people to be there when it is done — each hand off toward someone is held at the same distance, and someone across the table can meet a polished surface and not much else.

The fix here is not more practice. Put the problem down and step outside with nothing to solve. No one in mind, no plan. If something comes, note it and keep the feet moving. What you are having is not a failure of effort; the low setting is a door you have not used. Give it nothing to answer. Later you will be able to tell whether someone actually arrived, and that is all this requires.
cells.sheetLine: The work is steady. Nothing is expected in it anymore.

cells.tense: The practice is holding a room without knowing how the room got arranged.
cells.act: work the pattern through to its logic
cells.ask: Take one choice in your practice you are sure you made — the hour, the person, the thing you make room for — and reason it back to the moment you started it. Follow the pattern to where it begins, and name that.
cells.core:
You do not tell people you aimed this practice anywhere. One person keeps arriving into a room that was already warmed for them, and the weekly thing that brings them back goes on without a name on it. Somebody asks why it works and you say it just does.

It does not just do. That is a pattern, and its origin is you. Take one choice — the hour, the person, the thing you make room for — and reason it back to the moment you started it. Work the pattern through to its logic and name what you find at the start of it. That is a line of thought, not a speech. The weekly work takes its chosen source from you.
